rows.notes: Conceptual/policy perspective paper (HESS special issue) that posits three 'paradoxes' and illustrates them with three descriptive case narratives (Limari, Imperial Valley, Guadiana) built from secondary census statistics, agency reports and cited literature (e.g., Guadiana water savings reused for area expansion is attributed to AEVAL 2010 and Lopez-Gunn et al. 2012; Imperial transfer data from IID reports). The only author-generated analysis is a descriptive comparison of monthly streamflow and precipitation in the Limari Basin (Fig. 3), which concerns outlet flows, not drip-related savings; the authors explicitly state the record does not allow inference about the situation before efficiency increases and that they 'conjecture' flows were higher. No own experiment, survey, measurement campaign or validated model on drip irrigation and rebound; the link between drip adoption (Table 1: 0 to 60% of area in Limari) and area expansion is asserted from co-occurring statistics and the water-rights/subsidy framework rather than tested. Treated as not primary; if a reader counted the case narratives as own data, the evidence would still be descriptive and attributed largely to cited sources.

Same conceptual paper; the argument that efficiency gains reduce return flows supporting ecosystems (scale paradox) is stated as a conceptual assertion drawing on Perry (2011) and illustrated by cited reports (Salton Sea inflow decline from Case III et al. 2013; Guadiana wetland degradation from Blanco-Gutierrez et al. 2011, 2013; cross-border seepage loss from Maganda 2005). No own measurement of return flows, ecological flows, biodiversity or ecosystem services under drip versus flood; the Limari streamflow comparison (Fig. 3) is descriptive, not attributed to drip, and the authors acknowledge they cannot infer pre-efficiency conditions. Not a primary study on this claim.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The paper is a perspective/synthesis with illustrative case comparisons rather than a primary empirical study; classification of Q1 as 'no' follows the when-in-doubt rule, since the few author-compiled figures (Table 1, Fig. 3, Figs. 5-6) are descriptive secondary-statistics compilations and the key causal claims are either cited from other work or explicitly conjectured.
